title: Introduction & Basic Concepts
source: Cengel, Boles & Kanoglu — Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 1
summary:
**Thermodynamics** is the science of energy — its forms, its transformations, and the rules that govern them. The name fuses *therme* (heat) and *dynamis* (power), reflecting its origin in turning heat into work. Two pillars hold up everything that follows: the **first law** says energy is conserved (it changes form but is never created or destroyed), and the **second law** says energy has *quality* as well as quantity, and real processes always degrade that quality.

To analyse anything, you first draw a boundary. The **system** is the matter or region you choose to study; everything outside is the **surroundings**, and the **boundary** separates them. A **closed system** (control mass) keeps the same matter — energy may cross the boundary, but mass cannot. An **open system** (control volume) lets *both* mass and energy flow across; a nozzle, turbine or pipe section is analysed this way. An **isolated system** exchanges neither.

The condition of a system is described by its **properties**. *Intensive* properties (temperature, pressure, density) are independent of size; *extensive* properties (mass, total volume, total energy) scale with it. Divide an extensive property by mass and you get a **specific** property — itself intensive — such as specific volume $v = V/m$. A complete set of property values fixes the **state**; the **state postulate** says that for a simple compressible system, just *two* independent intensive properties are enough.

When properties stop changing, the system is in **equilibrium** (thermal, mechanical, phase and chemical). A **process** is any change of state, and the series of states it passes through is the **path**. The idealised **quasi-equilibrium** process stays infinitesimally close to equilibrium throughout — important because it is the kind of process we can draw on a diagram and for which work is well defined. A **cycle** returns the system to its initial state.

Finally, the chapter pins down two everyday-but-subtle properties. **Temperature** is grounded by the **zeroth law**: if two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in equilibrium with each other — which is what lets a thermometer work. **Pressure** is normal force per unit area; in a static fluid it rises with depth as $\Delta P = \rho g \Delta h$, the principle behind manometers and barometers. Throughout, keep your **units** consistent (SI: kg, m, s, N, Pa, J) — a surprising share of thermodynamics mistakes are really unit mistakes.

equations.name: Specific volume & density
equations.useWhen: Converting between total volume $V$ and mass $m$, or switching between density and specific volume — which you do constantly once property tables (which list $v$) enter the picture.
equations.note: Specific volume is volume per unit mass; it is the reciprocal of density $\rho$. Both are intensive.

equations.name: Specific gravity
equations.useWhen: A fluid is given by its specific gravity (e.g. manometer oil, $SG = 0.85$) and you need an actual density to use in $\rho g h$.
equations.note: Density relative to water at 4 °C ($\rho_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} \approx 1000\ \text{kg/m}^3$). Dimensionless.

equations.name: Celsius ↔ Kelvin
equations.useWhen: Before plugging temperature into *any* gas law or property relation. Reach for it automatically whenever a temperature appears in °C.
equations.note: A *temperature difference* is the same number in K and °C, so $\Delta T$ never needs converting.

equations.name: Pressure (definition)
equations.useWhen: A force is spread over an area — pistons, hydraulic lifts, a weight resting on a gas. Equate pressures across a piston to find an unknown force or area.
equations.note: Normal force per unit area. SI unit: pascal, $1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N/m}^2$. Bridge: $1\ \text{kPa·m}^3 = 1\ \text{kJ}$.

equations.name: Gauge & vacuum pressure
equations.useWhen: A pressure comes from a gauge or is labelled "vacuum". Convert to absolute *first*, because every property relation needs absolute pressure.
equations.note: Gauges read relative to local atmospheric pressure; $P_{\text{vac}} = P_{\text{atm}} - P_{\text{abs}}$.

equations.name: Hydrostatic pressure variation
equations.useWhen: Pressure changes with depth in a static liquid — dams, tanks, finding a depth from a pressure difference.
equations.note: Pressure is the same at all points on a horizontal level within a connected static fluid.

equations.name: Manometer relation
equations.useWhen: Reading a gas/vessel pressure off a liquid column height $h$, or the reverse. Barometer is the special case $P_{\text{atm}} = \rho g h$.
equations.note: Add a $\rho g h$ term going *down* each fluid column and subtract going *up*.

glossary.definition: The science of energy and its transformations, built on conservation of energy (first law) and the direction/quality of processes (second law).
The quantity of matter or region in space chosen for study.
Everything outside the system is the *surroundings*; the real or imaginary surface separating them is the *boundary* (it can be fixed or movable).
A fixed amount of matter: energy can cross the boundary, but mass cannot.
A region that both mass and energy can flow into and out of — e.g. a nozzle, turbine, or compressor.
A system that exchanges neither mass nor energy with its surroundings.
Any characteristic of a system (e.g. $P$, $T$, $V$, $m$). *Intensive* properties are size-independent; *extensive* properties scale with mass.
An extensive property per unit mass (e.g. specific volume $v = V/m$); it is itself intensive.
The set of all property values at a given condition. For a simple compressible system, two independent intensive properties fix the state.
No unbalanced potentials within the system: thermal, mechanical, phase and chemical equilibrium together give *thermodynamic equilibrium*.
A *process* is a change from one state to another; the *path* is the series of states passed through.
An idealised process that remains infinitesimally close to equilibrium throughout, so it can be drawn on property diagrams and yields the maximum work output.
A process (or series of processes) that returns the system to its initial state.
If two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other — the basis of temperature measurement.
Normal force exerted by a fluid per unit area. Distinguish *absolute*, *gauge*, and *vacuum* pressure.
The assumption that matter is continuously distributed, so properties like density are defined at a point — valid when the mean free path is small relative to the system.

tips: **Convert to absolute units first.** Gas laws and property tables need absolute temperature (K) and absolute pressure — not °C or gauge pressure. This is the single most common Ch 1 mistake.
**Gauge vs absolute pressure.** A tyre gauge reading 200 kPa means $P_{\text{abs}} \approx 301$ kPa. Add $P_{\text{atm}}$ unless the problem already gives absolute pressure.
**Intensive vs extensive.** If doubling the amount of substance doubles the quantity, it's extensive (mass, volume, energy). Dividing by mass turns it intensive (a *specific* property).
**Watch your unit bridges.** $1\ \text{N} = 1\ \text{kg·m/s}^2$ and $1\ \text{kJ} = 1\ \text{kPa·m}^3$. Carrying units through the algebra catches most numerical errors.
**Quasi-equilibrium is an idealisation.** Real fast processes are *not* quasi-equilibrium; you only get to draw a smooth path and compute reversible work when the process is (assumed) quasi-static.
